questions.q: What are the five elements this lesson's template requires for a trustworthy QML experiment write-up?
options: Exact setup, exact classical baseline and how it was chosen, exact measured numbers, what varied between runs, and an explicit statement of what does/doesn't generalize
A marketing-style summary emphasizing the most favorable possible interpretation
Only the final accuracy number, with no other details required
The dataset name alone, since that implies everything else
questions.explain: The lesson's template requires exact setup details, baseline justification, precise unrounded measured numbers, sources of run-to-run variation, and explicit scope limits on what the result does and doesn't generalize to.

questions.q: Applying the template to this course's own Chapter 6 project, what is the HONEST description of the quantum classifier's training setup?
options: Only one gradient-descent step on one training sample (Setosa), evaluated on a 6-sample held-out set -- not a full multi-sample, multi-iteration training run
A model trained on real hardware rather than simulation
A model trained using 10-fold cross-validation with hyperparameter tuning
A fully trained model using hundreds of iterations across the entire Iris dataset
questions.explain: The honest setup description acknowledges the training was minimal -- one gradient step, one sample -- which is exactly why the 50% accuracy result needs careful, scoped interpretation rather than being treated as a mature benchmark.

questions.q: What does the lesson say the 50% vs 100% result from Lesson 25 does NOT license concluding?
options: That quantum classifiers underperform classical ones on Iris-like tasks in general, or anything about QML's practical advantage on real-world problems generally
That the quantum classifier predicted class 0 for every held-out sample
That only one gradient step was taken during training
That the classical threshold rule achieved 100% accuracy on the held-out set
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly distinguishes the narrow, accurate finding (one undertrained run underperformed a trivial baseline) from any broader, unsupported generalization about QML's capability or practical advantage -- exactly the distinction Chapter 1 asked readers to maintain throughout.

questions.q: Why does the lesson argue that an honest mixed or negative result report is MORE valuable than an enthusiastic, favorable-sounding one?
options: A precise, reproducible, falsifiable report respects the reader's ability to check the reasoning, while a vague favorable-sounding claim is easy to overstate into something it isn't
Enthusiastic reports are factually required to be false
Negative results are always more mathematically interesting than positive ones
There is no real difference in value between the two types of reports
questions.explain: The lesson values precision and falsifiability over favorable framing -- a report detailing exact setup, baseline, numbers, and scope lets others verify, extend, or correct the work, which is the actual mark of a useful result.

questions.q: How does this closing lesson explicitly connect back to Lesson 1's framing of QML as 'an open research question'?
options: It proves Lesson 1's framing was overly cautious and QML has already demonstrated clear advantage
It reverses Lesson 1's framing, concluding that QML has now been proven to have no practical use
It has no connection to Lesson 1; the two lessons address unrelated topics

The Chapter 6 project itself models calibrated uncertainty in practice -- building something real, measuring it fairly, getting an unflattering result, and reporting it precisely without excusing it away or overgeneralizing it
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly frames the whole Chapter 6 project as a small, concrete demonstration of the calibrated-uncertainty posture Lesson 1 asked for -- real work, fair measurement, honest reporting, without hype or dismissal in either direction.
